newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia plans $146.8 mln late payments to farmers.
newsitem.headline: Serbia plans $146.8 mln late payments to farmers.

text.p: The Serbian government presented on Thursday a plan to clear an outstanding 800 million dinar ($146.8 million) debt to farmers to prevent a boycott of spring sowings.

"Serbia showed its goodwill and made extraordinary efforts to secure the means for financing its due liabilities considering the general cash shortage in the entire economy," deputy agriculture minister Srboljub Stankovic told a news conference.
Around 425.5 million is owed for sugar beet, 266.9 million for sunflower, 61.41 million for tobacco and 46.2 million for grapes.
The government set March 15 as a deadline for clearing its sugar beet and sunfower debts, and the end of April for tobacco and grapes payments.
Industry sources said farmers, who had already threatened to boycott sugar beet spring plantings, were unlikely to accept another postponement.
Serbia intends to clear late payments partly in cash and partly in exchange for fuel and fertiliser.
The government expects sugar, oils, tobacco and wine producers to secure 400 million dinars in cash by selling their products home and abroad.
"It is necessary to boost exports of these goods within existing gas and oil barter deals (with Russia and China)," Stankovic said.
The National Bank of Yugoslavia (NBY) is expected to secure another 200 million dinars.
"NBY could either use reserve requirement or issue non-inflationary forward contracts with agricultural produce as collateral," said Serbian assistant finance minister Garip Hadzini.
The Yugoslav and Serbian commodity reserve agencies should provide 50 million dinars each by selling goods from their stocks.
The last 100 million dinars would be secured from Serbia's agriculture budget, Hadzini said.
Analysts warned earlier that delayed payments to farmers could affect this year's spring sowing campaign.
Agricultural cooperatives have called on members not to sign any new contracts with processing industries if they are not paid what is owed to them.
Serbia said it planned about 2.36 million hectares of spring sowings, or about 64 percent of the total arable area.
Some 1.4 million hectares should be sown with maize, 408,000 with industrial crops, 250,000 to vegetables and 182,000 with fodder crops.
According to some estimates, around three billion dinars are needed to complete spring sowings, of which some 40 percent needs to be pre-financed.
